headline: Medium risk: Pipecat’s shared-bus, API-calling defaults can amplify Dagster outputs into leakage or cascading errors, while direct prompt-injection and filesystem conflict are limited by Dagster’s no-IO profile.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dagster has no clipboard, stdin/stdout, filesystem read/write, MCP, or browser surfaces, so it cannot ingest Pipecat output by default. Pipecat does expose stdin/stdout and shared-bus concurrency, but without a bridge from Dagster there is no plausible injection path in this pair.
conditions: IF Dagster is wrapped in an external process that copies Pipecat text into a trusted parser, injection becomes plausible.
IF a shared bus is added between the agents, attacker-controlled Pipecat content can reach Dagster.
IF Dagster gains file or stdin ingestion, prompt-injection risk changes from none to at least low.
mitigations: Keep Dagster isolated from Pipecat text channels.
Do not pipe Pipecat transcripts into Dagster parsers.
Add provenance tags before any manual copy-paste bridge.
requires-engineering: introduce a sanitizer/allowlist for any future shared bus.
requires-engineering: add explicit trust boundaries in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dagster touches no data classes and has no network egress, but Pipecat processes audio, video, images, text, and conversation state and can call many third-party APIs. If Dagster outputs are fed into Pipecat’s shared bus or API-backed services, sensitive work products can leak in default Pipecat-style deployments.
conditions: IF Dagster outputs contain sensitive text and are forwarded into Pipecat services, leakage occurs.
IF Pipecat is configured with any external STT/LLM/TTS provider, content may leave the local boundary.
IF both agents share a workspace or bus, accidental disclosure becomes more likely.
mitigations: Keep sensitive Dagster outputs out of Pipecat inputs.
Use local-only Pipecat providers where possible.
Disable unnecessary Pipecat API connectors.
Separate workspaces and credentials per agent.
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before Pipecat egress.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Dagster cannot write the filesystem, modify git, or use MCP, so it cannot contend for mutable local resources. Pipecat supports shared-bus session state and multiple instances, but the pair lacks overlapping write surfaces in the profiles, making conflict unlikely and limited.
conditions: IF Dagster is given filesystem write or git privileges later, write conflicts become possible.
IF Pipecat instances are pointed at the same mutable external resource, contention can arise.
IF an orchestrator removes Pipecat bus isolation, shared-state races may appear.
mitigations: Keep Dagster read-only.
Avoid sharing mutable resources between Pipecat instances.
Run one Pipecat session per bus namespace.
requires-engineering: add locking around any future shared writes.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent resource namespaces.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Pipecat can consume and relay text through shared-bus sessions and many API-backed services, so if Dagster-produced outputs are treated as authoritative upstream facts, errors can cascade into downstream speech or LLM actions. Dagster itself is an orchestrator, but the pair lacks a documented verification step between them.
conditions: IF Dagster outputs are forwarded to Pipecat without validation, errors can propagate.
IF Pipecat uses those outputs to drive LLM or TTS responses, the cascade reaches end users.
IF no verification layer is inserted between the agents, false facts can be amplified.
mitigations: Insert a validation step before Pipecat consumes Dagster output.
Require schema checks on all Dagster-to-Pipecat messages.
Log and review a sample of cross-agent handoffs.
Use human approval for high-impact downstream actions.
requires-engineering: add confidence gating and provenance tracking.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention commitments shown. Pipecat’s many external API connectors create a compliance surface, but Dagster itself shows no data classes touched or egress. The main issue is documented gaps rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through Pipecat’s third-party connectors, compliance obligations increase.
IF the deployment requires residency or retention guarantees, the current profiles do not document them.
IF sensitive data classes are introduced later, the compliance assessment must be revisited.
mitigations: Review provider DPAs before enabling external connectors.
Keep regulated data out of Pipecat API calls.
Document retention and deletion settings.
Separate compliant and non-compliant workloads.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention.
